 Two Social Security Checks Become One When a Husband Dies. A Widow Keeps the Larger of the Two, and the Household Loses the Smaller
 By Jake FitzGerald 
 Published November 18, 2026, 3:05pm ET · 4 min read 
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 When a husband dies, a widow keeps the larger Social Security check and loses the smaller, cutting household benefits about 40% while rent and utilities stay put.
 A widow's tax thresholds shrink faster than her income: the single base is $25,000 versus $32,000 joint, so her unchanged IRA withdrawal gets taxed more.
 Survivor benefits start at 71.5% of the late spouse's benefit and reach 100% at full retirement age, between 66 and 67.

 When a married retiree dies, the household’s two Social Security deposits become one. The widow keeps whichever check is larger, and the lower one stops. Rent, property taxes, insurance and utilities usually stay about the same. Using Social Security Administration averages for 2026, a typical retired couple loses about 40% of its Social Security income when it becomes a one-person household.
 How SSA Decides Which Check She Keeps
 Someone who qualifies for both her own retirement benefit and a survivor benefit on her husband’s record receives one payment. SSA says she chooses the payment that works best for her and that “the payments won’t be added together.” [ 1 ] She can also switch later. SSA’s own example is starting on survivor benefits and moving to her own retirement benefit at age 70 [ 1 ] if that payment is higher by then.
 When she claims affects how much she gets. Survivor payments start at 71.5% [ 1 ] of the late spouse’s benefit and rise the longer she waits. They reach up to 100% [ 1 ] at her full retirement age for survivor benefits, which falls between ages 66 and 67. By her early 70s, she is already past that age, so a survivor claim filed now carries no reduction for her age.
 Survivor claiming has its own rules, its own full retirement age, and its own switching options, and getting the sequence wrong can cost a widow six figures over a retirement. We walked through the survivor benefit math couples should run before 70, available here: Widow’s Math .
 Timing around the death also matters. SSA’s survivors toolkit states that if the deceased was receiving benefits, “any benefits received for the month of death and any later months are not due and must be returned.” [ 2 ] She should plan on that deposit going back. Separately, a spouse or some minor children can receive a one-time death payment of $255 [ 1 ] . IRS Publication 525 for tax year 2025 confirms lump-sum death benefits are exempt from federal income tax.
 One Household, Before and After
 The example below uses the 2026 average monthly benefit that the Social Security Administration projects for an senior couple with both spouses receiving benefits, and for an senior widow living alone. It assumes the household also takes out $20,000 a year from an IRA. Tax figures are for tax year 2026.

 Social Security income falls by $1,289 a month, or $15,468 a year. The taxable part of her benefits barely moves, going from $3,624 to $3,257. As a share of benefits, the taxed part rises from about 9.4% to about 14.1%.
 Why Her Tax Thresholds Shrink Faster Than Her Income
 Under 26 U.S.C. § 86(c) [ 3 ] , Social Security starts becoming taxable once combined income passes a base amount of $25,000 [ 3 ] for individual taxpayers, compared with $32,000 on a joint return. A second level starts at an adjusted base amount of $34,000 [ 3 ] for individual filers and $44,000 on a joint return. Above that level, up to 85% [ 3 ] of benefits can be taxed. The single base amount is more than half the joint figure, so halving the married number gives the wrong answer. Her IRA withdrawal stays the same size while the threshold it is measured against drops.
 Filing status changes on a set schedule. IRS Publication 17 says a widow who has not remarried is considered married for the whole year her spouse died and can file jointly for that year. This filing status covers 2 years after the death, but only for a widow with a child she can claim as a dependent living in her home. Someone in her early 70s with grown children generally files single starting the year after the death.
 What to Watch Heading Into 2027
 A 3.6% COLA is set for 2027. It raises her one left check, along with the combined income that is measured against the $25,000 [ 3 ] base. The research price index for Americans 62 and older reached 368.804 [ 4 ] in October 2026, the high of the past year. That index gives heavy weight to housing and medical care, two costs that stay about the same after a death. Over the longer term, the 2026 [ 5 ] Trustees Report projects the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance trust fund will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032. At that point, 78% [ 5 ] of scheduled benefits would remain payable.
